docs.title: Modeling with patterns
docs.text:
Welcome to the tutorial on modeling with patterns in torch_structure. If you have not installed torch_structure yet or had problems with the installation process, please refer to the installation guide.

TorchStructure's patterns all work in similar ways. First, we will start with a rotational pattern.

docs.title: A rotational pattern
docs.text:
We start by creating an empty StructData graph whose nodes carry 3D coordinates.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs)

Next, we create a 6-fold rotational pattern and register it on the graph under the name "rotation". By default, it rotates about the z-axis through the origin. Adding a single node (the seed) with add_nodes_by_pattern then also adds its five rotated copies.

rotation = data.create_rotational_pattern(6)
data.add_patterns({"rotation": rotation})

data.add_nodes_by_pattern(pattern="rotation", coords=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]]))

Visualize the result. With pattern=True, plot draws the nodes together with the pattern.

data.plot(pattern=True)
plt.show()

Edges work the same way. Adding an edge from the first node to the second with add_edges_by_pattern also adds its five rotated copies, which connect the six nodes into a hexagon.

data.add_edges_by_pattern(edge_indices=torch.tensor([[0], [1]]))

The six nodes stay linked through the pattern: if we move one of them, the other five adjust, and the edges follow. Here, we move the first node outwards from (1, 0, 0) to (2, 0, 0) with set_node_attr_by_pattern, where mask selects the node to move. Edge attributes can be set in a similar manner with set_edge_attr_by_pattern, which gives all rotated copies of the selected edge the same value.

mask = torch.tensor([True, False, False, False, False, False])
data.set_node_attr_by_pattern("coords", mask=mask, value=torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0, 0.0]]))

To move a single node without its copies, use set_node_attr instead of set_node_attr_by_pattern. Here, we move the first node slightly inwards, while the other five nodes stay where they are.

data.set_node_attr("coords", mask=mask, value=torch.tensor([[1.6, 0.0, 0.0]]))

docs.title: A translational pattern
docs.text:
We again start with an empty StructData graph whose nodes carry 3D coordinates.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs)

Next, we create a translational pattern with 4 positions and register it on the graph under the name "translation". By default, each position is shifted by (1, 0, 0) from the previous one. Adding a single node (the seed) with add_nodes_by_pattern then also adds its three shifted copies, which gives an array of 4 nodes. We again add an edge from the first node to the second.

translation = data.create_translational_pattern(4)
data.add_patterns({"translation": translation})

data.add_nodes_by_pattern(pattern="translation", coords=torch.tensor([[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]]))
data.add_edges_by_pattern(edge_indices=torch.tensor([[0], [1]]))

Visualize the result. With pattern=True, plot draws the nodes and edges together with the pattern, each translation step as an arrow.

data.plot(pattern=True)
plt.show()

The nodes stay linked through the pattern. Changing one node changes the others accordingly.

mask = torch.tensor([True, False, False, False])
data.set_node_attr_by_pattern("coords", mask=mask, value=torch.tensor([[0.0, 1.0, 0.0]]))

docs.title: Nesting patterns
docs.text: Patterns can be nested with nest_patterns: each pattern copies everything the patterns before it created. Nesting a translation with a rotation can give very different structures, depending on the direction of the translation.

docs.title: A polar net
docs.text:
We start with a 4-fold translation along the x-axis nested into a 6-fold rotation to get a polar net of 4 × 6 = 24 nodes. As copies of one seed, they form one expansion (id 0), where each node has a position on every pattern level, innermost pattern first: e.g. [1, 0] is one translation step out, [0, 1] one rotation step around, and [3, 2] 3 translation steps out and 2 rotation steps around. add_edges_by_pattern_level connects such positions. An edge from [0, 0] to [1, 0] runs outwards along the first array.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs)

translation = data.create_translational_pattern(4, direction=torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
rotation = data.create_rotational_pattern(6)
data.add_patterns({"polar_net": data.nest_patterns([translation, rotation])})

data.add_nodes_by_pattern(pattern="polar_net", coords=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]]))
data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[1, 0]],
)

Visualize the result.

data.plot(pattern=True)
plt.show()

We could equally give the edge by the indices of its two nodes, with add_edges_by_pattern as in the sections above, or by their positions in the expansion, with add_edges_per_expansion_by_pattern. Here, both count the nodes translation by translation, from the inside out, so the level positions [t, r] are node and expansion position t + 4 * r. In place of the call above, either of these would add the same edges:

data.add_edges_by_pattern(edge_indices=torch.tensor([[0], [1]]))

data.add_edges_per_expansion_by_pattern(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_expansion_positions=[0], dest_expansion_positions=[1],
)

Next, we add an edge in the rotational direction, from level positions [0, 0] to [0, 1]. Its copies connect nodes in the rotational direction.

data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[0, 1]],
)

Finally, we add an edge in the diagonal direction, from [0, 0] to [1, 1].

data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[1, 1]],
)

Nested patterns stay linked as well. Here, we move the outermost ring outwards, from a radius of 4 to 5, with set_node_attr_by_pattern_level, which selects a node by its level positions just like add_edges_by_pattern_level: [3, 0] is the last node of the first array. replicate_levels takes one entry per level of the pattern, innermost first: [False, True] freezes the inner pattern (the translation), so the move is copied around the ring but not along the translations. replicate_levels=[True, True] would move every ring outwards, and replicate_levels=[True, False] would only move one array.

data.set_node_attr_by_pattern_level(
    "coords", expansion_ids=[0], level_positions=[[3, 0]],
    value=torch.tensor([[5.0, 0.0, 0.0]]), replicate_levels=[False, True],
)

docs.title: A cylinder
docs.text:
If the translation instead runs along the rotation axis, it stacks the seed into a column of 4 nodes, and the same rotation copies this column into a cylinder of 4 × 6 = 24 nodes. This time, we start with an edge in the rotational direction, from [0, 0] to [0, 1]. Its copies connect the nodes at each height into a closed ring, which gives 4 × 6 = 24 edges.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs)

translation = data.create_translational_pattern(4, direction=torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]))
rotation = data.create_rotational_pattern(6)
data.add_patterns({"cylinder": data.nest_patterns([translation, rotation])})

data.add_nodes_by_pattern(pattern="cylinder", coords=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]]))
data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[0, 1]],
)

Visualize the result.

data.plot(pattern=True)
plt.show()

Again, we could equally give this edge by node index or by expansion position. Both now count the nodes column by column, from the bottom up, so [0, 1] is node and expansion position 4. In place of the call above, either of these would add the same 24 edges:

data.add_edges_by_pattern(edge_indices=torch.tensor([[0], [4]]))

data.add_edges_per_expansion_by_pattern(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_expansion_positions=[0], dest_expansion_positions=[4],
)

Next, we add an edge in the translational direction, from [0, 0] to [1, 0], one step up the first column. Its copies connect the nodes of every column.

data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[1, 0]],
)

Finally, we add an edge in the diagonal direction, from [0, 0] to [1, 1].

data.add_edges_by_pattern_level(
    src_expansion_ids=[0], dest_expansion_ids=[0],
    src_level_positions=[[0, 0]], dest_level_positions=[[1, 1]],
)

set_node_attr_by_pattern_level with replicate_levels=[False, True] again replicates the changed value of a node around the ring, but not up the columns.

data.set_node_attr_by_pattern_level(
    "coords", expansion_ids=[0], level_positions=[[1, 0]],
    value=torch.tensor([[1.2, 0.0, 1.0]]), replicate_levels=[False, True],
)

docs.title: Plotting structures
docs.text:
Every StructData object can draw itself with data.plot(). The same function is available as plot_structure in torch_structure.plot, so data.plot(...) and plot_structure(data, ...) are interchangeable.

This page explains what is drawn by default, and how to color, size and label edges and nodes by any of their attributes.

docs.title: The default plot
docs.text:
data.plot(show=True)

Without any arguments, plot draws what the structure in a way you might be used to seeing it:

  • Edges: every undirected edge is drawn once. If the structure has a force attribute, edges in tension are red, edges in compression blue and edges without force gray, and the line width grows with the magnitude of the force.
  • Supports: nodes with is_support are drawn as black circles, or as squares when they also restrain rotations (support_rxyz).
  • Nodes are not drawn by default, see Nodes.

The legend lists everything that was drawn. plot returns the matplotlib axis, so you can keep adding to the figure, and the show=True argument displays it. To save the figure, pass a path: data.plot(path="cable_net") writes cable_net.png.

docs.title: Loads and reactions
docs.text:
loads=True draws the load attribute as green arrows starting at their nodes:

data.plot(loads=True, vector_scale=1.5, edge_width=0.8)

reactions=True draws the reaction_force attribute as orange arrows.

data.plot(reactions=True, vector_scale=0.0025, edge_width=0.8)

Both also take another attribute name or a tensor of shape [num_nodes, 3]. Any other node vectors are drawn with vectors, a dictionary from legend label to attribute name or tensor:

data.plot(vectors={"Residual": residual_force})

The length of an arrow shows the magnitude of its force: all arrows in a plot share one scale, by default chosen so that the longest arrow is 15 % of the structure's size. vector_scale sets the arrow length per unit of force instead.

docs.title: Coloring by an attribute
docs.text:
edge_color and node_color take the name of an attribute. How its values are turned into colors depends on their type.

Floating-point numbers get a colormap and a colorbar, as do integers with more than 10 different values:

data.plot(edge_color="force")

When the values have both signs, the colormap is diverging and centred on zero. Use cmap to choose another colormap and clim=(low, high) to fix its range.

Integers with at most 10 different values are treated as categories, each with its own color and legend entry. This suits ids such as a material_id:

data.plot(edge_color="material_id")

Booleans highlight the True entries, e.g. edge_color="is_boundary_edge".

A plain color draws everything in that color: edge_color="black".

Instead of an attribute name, you can also pass the values directly as a tensor. This is handy for quantities that are not stored on the graph:

data.plot(edge_color=data.length_from_coords)

Directed and undirected edges

StructData stores every edge in both directions. Edge values can be given for all directed edges, as stored, or for every undirected edge once, e.g. data.force[data.directed_mask.view(-1)]. plot recognizes both by their length.

docs.title: Line widths
docs.text:
edge_width works like edge_color: an attribute name or values, whose magnitude sets the width, or a constant width.

data.plot(edge_width="force_density")   # wider edges for larger force densities
data.plot(edge_width=1.0)               # every edge equally thin

lw_scale sets the global line width scale for all edges.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
view selects a 3D view or a 2D projection:

view shows "3d" (default) an axonometric 3D view "xy" the plan "xz" the elevation along x "yz" the elevation along y

Projections are often easier to read for planar structures such as trusses and arches. All axes share one scale unless equal_axes=False, and show_axes=True adds axis lines and labels.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
Nodes are drawn as soon as you give them a color or size. Both take the same kinds of values as the edges:

data.height = data.coords[:, 2:]
data.plot(view="xy", edge_color="black", edge_width=0.8, node_color="height")

node_size takes a constant marker size, or an attribute whose magnitude sets the size.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
node_labels writes text at each node and edge_labels at each edge's midpoint:

  • "index": the node index, or the edge's row in edge_index;
  • "name" (nodes only): the node names given in add_node;
  • an attribute name or values, formatted with label_format (default "{:.3g}"); attributes with several components, such as "coords", are written as tuples;
  • a list of strings, one per node or edge, where empty strings are left out.
data.plot(view="xy", edge_color="grey", edge_width=0.8, node_labels="index")

docs.title: Comparing with a reference geometry
docs.text:
ghost draws a second geometry, dashed and gray, behind the structure. It takes other coordinates for the same structure, such as the geometry before form finding or a target shape, or a different StructData object.

data.plot(ghost=initial_coords, ghost_label="Initial geometry", edge_color="black", edge_width=0.8)

To plot the structure itself at other coordinates, pass them as coords, e.g. data.plot(coords=result.coords, ghost=data.coords, ghost_label="Undeformed").

docs.title: Showing part of a structure
docs.text:
edge_mask and node_mask select what is drawn, as a boolean mask or a list of indices:

data.plot(edge_mask=data.force.view(-1) > 0)        # only the edges in tension
data.plot(node_mask=[0, 5, 12], node_labels="index")  # label three nodes

node_mask applies to the nodes, their labels, supports and arrows; the edges are drawn regardless.

docs.title: Combining plots
docs.text:
Because plot returns its axis and accepts one with ax, several plots can be drawn into one figure. Plots on the same axis are overlaid, and the legend keeps the entries of each:

ax = before.plot(edge_color="grey")
after.plot(ax=ax, title="Before and after")

For side-by-side plots, create the axes yourself. Use a 3D axis for the 3D view and a 2D axis for projections:

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
data.plot(ax=fig.add_subplot(121, projection="3d"))
data.plot(ax=fig.add_subplot(122), view="xz")

The API reference describes every argument in full.

docs.title: Creating topologies
docs.text:
Welcome to the topology creation tutorial for torch_structure. If you have not installed torch_structure yet or had problems with the installation process, please refer to the installation guide.

TorchStructure's topology functions all follow the same template. First, we will start with a simple chain.

docs.title: A simple chain
docs.text:
We start by creating an empty StructData graph. Node and edge attributes are registered as dictionaries of empty tensors, where the tensor shape defines the attribute's dimension. In this example, nodes carry 3D coordinates and edges have a material id.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
edge_attrs = {"material_id": torch.empty((0,1), dtype=torch.long)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs, edge_attrs=edge_attrs)
Values for node and edge attributes are also assigned via dictionaries, with attribute names as keys and either tensors or callables as values. The details of how the callables work are explained below. For now, it suffices to understand that node coordinates are computed by callable compute_coordinates that takes unit coordinates in x-direction as an input and maps them to a parabolic arch. A uniform edge material id is set directly with a tensor.

num_nodes = 10

material_id = torch.ones(num_nodes - 1, 1, dtype=torch.long)

def compute_coordinates(x_unit_coord):
    height = 3 * x_unit_coord * (1 - x_unit_coord)
    return torch.hstack([x_unit_coord, torch.zeros_like(x_unit_coord), height])

node_attrs = {"coords": compute_coordinates}
edge_attrs = {"material_id": material_id}

data.add_chain(num_nodes, node_attrs=node_attrs, edge_attrs=edge_attrs)

Visualize the result. The plot function automatically recognizes the coords attributes and realizes the graph based on it. The material_id attribute has no impact on the plot, as it is just information stored on the graph. 

data.plot()
plt.show()

docs.title: A grid
docs.text:
A grid has N = n × m nodes and E = n(m-1) + m(n-1) edges. We register the same attributes as before and create an empty StructData object.

import torch
from torch_structure.data.data import StructData
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

node_attrs = {"coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float)}
edge_attrs = {"material_id": torch.empty((0, 1), dtype=torch.long)}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs, edge_attrs=edge_attrs)

In a similar fashion as before, node coordinates are set with a callable that uses both x_unit_coord and y_unit_coord, mapping the unit square to a tonne (barrel vault) shape: arched along x with a shallow curve, and straight along y. Edge attributes are again a constant tensor.

num_rows, num_cols = 10, 10
num_edges = num_rows * (num_cols - 1) + num_cols * (num_rows - 1)

material_id = torch.ones(num_edges, 1, dtype=torch.long)

def compute_coordinates(x_unit_coord, y_unit_coord):
    height = 1.2 * x_unit_coord * (1 - x_unit_coord)
    return torch.hstack([x_unit_coord, y_unit_coord, height])

node_attrs = {"coords": compute_coordinates}
edge_attrs = {"material_id": material_id}

data.add_grid(num_rows, num_cols, node_attrs=node_attrs, edge_attrs=edge_attrs)

Visualize the result. 

data.plot()
plt.show()

docs.title: The general pattern
docs.text:
All topology functions (add_chain, add_grid, add_triangular_grid, add_polar_grid) follow the same pattern.

Their input consists of node_attrs and edge_attrs as arguments for the graph's attributes as well as some integers to specify the topology's resolution. The amount of these integers corresponds to their shape parameters. E.g. a grid is determined by two, an isosceles triangle by one shape parameter.

The dictionary keys have to be any of the attributes specified when the graph is created. Attributes that are not in node_attrs or edge_attrs but were registered in the graph at creation, will be filled with default values or, if none were specified, with zeros.

The dictionary values are either a tensor or a callable that returns a tensor. In both cases the resulting tensor must have shape [N, *] for node attributes or [E, *] for edge attributes, where the trailing dimensions match those registered on the StructData object for the same attribute. For a tensor as a dictionary value, a shape of [1, *] is also accepted and broadcast uniformly over all nodes or edges.

docs.title: How callables work
docs.text:
When a dictionary value is a callable, torch_structure resolves its inputs by name. It inspects the callable's parameter names and passes the matching tensors as arguments. Two sources are available:

  • Default attributes: each topology function pre-computes a set of suitable attributes (node indices, unit coordinates, boundary flags, etc.) that can be used directly as callable inputs. See the API reference for the full list per function.

  • Previously defined attributes: any attribute already set earlier in the same dictionary is also available as a callable input. This allows attributes to be built up step by step — for example, registering height first and then passing it into the callable that computes coords:

    node_attrs = {
    "height": torch.empty((0, 1), dtype=torch.float),
    "coords": torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.float),
}
data = StructData(node_attrs=node_attrs)

def get_height(x_unit_coord):
    return 3 * x_unit_coord * (1 - x_unit_coord)

def get_coords(x_unit_coord, height):
    return torch.hstack([x_unit_coord, torch.zeros_like(x_unit_coord), height])

node_attrs = {
    "height": get_height,
    "coords": get_coords,
}
data.add_chain(10, node_attrs=node_attrs)

The callable's return value is subject to the same dimension requirements as a direct tensor. If you want to use default attributes, make sure the arguments of your callable match the default attribute names specified in the API reference exactly.
